stories.headline: NBA Power Rankings: How all 30 teams stack up after one week
stories.summary: Here's where all 30 NBA teams rank after one week of the 2026-27 regular season, plus the most surprising statistic or trend for each franchise.
stories.body:
It's been a little over a week since the start of the 2026-27 NBA regular season, and we've already had a jam-packed couple of days filled with surprise starts, star returns and a few disappointing debuts.

LeBron James kicked off his 24th season with the new-look Philadelphia 76ers by defeating the defending champs -- the New York Knicks -- after their ring ceremony at Madison Square Garden and displaying early positive returns following a busy offseason.

On the flip side, the San Antonio Spurs, after a Finals appearance in June, are struggling behind young superstar Victor Wembanyama. However, their cross-state rivals, the Houston Rockets, are one of four undefeated teams left in the Western Conference, along with the Oklahoma City Thunder (the 2024-25 champions), the Memphis Grizzlies and the Portland Trail Blazers.

In our first iteration of Power Rankings this campaign, our NBA insiders break down their biggest observations from opening week, including the most surprising statistic or trend for every team, and what to expect as teams try to find their footing or build on their momentum.

Note: Team rankings are based on where members of our panel (ESPN's Jamal Collier, Michael C. Wright, Tim MacMahon, Dave McMenamin, Vincent Goodwill, Zach Kram, Ben Golliver, Kris Rhim and Anthony Slater) think teams belong.

Previous rankings: Preseason

Jump to a team:

ATL | BOS | BKN | CHA | CHI | CLE

DAL | DEN | DET | GS | HOU | IND

LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN

NO | NY | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX

POR | SAC | SA | TOR | UTAH | WAS

1. Oklahoma City Thunder

2026-27 record: 4-0
Previous ranking: 1
Next games: @ DAL (Oct. 28), @ HOU (Oct. 31), @ CLE (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: Third-year guard Ajay Mitchell's elevated role. In the wake of the serious injuries suffered by Jalen Williams (fibula/ankle) and Cason Wallace (shoulder), Mitchell should see an increased role on the floor. He has repeatedly shown that he can thrive as the No. 2 offensive option alongside two-time MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. Mitchell averaged 22.5 points and 6.0 assists in the Thunder's sweep of the Lakers in last season's Western Conference semifinals, when Williams was sidelined. Mitchell had a career-high 30 points and five assists in Monday's win over the Suns, his first start of the season. -- Tim MacMahon

2. Minnesota Timberwolves

2026-27 record: 3-1
Previous ranking: 5
Next games: vs. GS (Oct. 28), vs. LAC (Oct. 30), @ SA (Oct. 31), vs. MIL (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 120.8 offensive rating. Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball's instant chemistry was marvelous: Minnesota's new-look starting lineup outscored opponents by 31 points in 56 minutes through four games. Meanwhile, the Timberwolves posted a 120.8 offensive rating when their dynamic guard duo shared the court -- an exceptional mark that would have ranked second in the NBA last season. However, that could all come to a halt as Edwards will be sidelined up to two months, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania on Tuesday because of an arthroscopic procedure on his right knee. -- Ben Golliver

3. Detroit Pistons

2026-27 record: 3-1
Previous ranking: 7
Next games: vs. CHA (Oct. 28), @ BKN (Oct. 30), @ CHA (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 42%. That's what the previously anemic Pistons have shot from 3 in the first three games this season. Duncan Robinson leads the league in makes per game (5.0) and is shooting a blistering 54% from distance, while newcomer John Collins is taking nearly five a night at a 50% clip. Last season, this team was barely near the league average and struggled at creating and making shots in the playoffs, leading to their second-round loss to Cleveland. Head coach J.B. Bickerstaff said Robinson is more comfortable looking for shots and taking contested ones, which also means some regression to the mean will occur. But being more aggressive is a positive sign of sorts. -- Vincent Goodwill

4. Houston Rockets

2026-27 record: 4-0
Previous ranking: 10
Next games: @ MIL (Oct. 28), @ DAL (Oct. 30), vs. OKC (Oct. 31), vs. BOS (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 4-0 start. For the first time since 2014-15, Houston is off to a 4-0 start and finally playing the way it was expected to last season when it first acquired Kevin Durant. The return of veteran point guard Fred VanVleet, who missed last season with a torn ACL, has played a role in Durant starting off the season with four straight 20-point games for the 10th time in his career. Meanwhile, big man Alperen Sengun is feasting off the order VanVleet has restored to the offense, becoming just the third Rocket to put together multiple 25-5-5 games within the first four games of the season. -- Michael C. Wright

5. Philadelphia 76ers

2026-27 record: 3-1
Previous ranking: 4
Next games: @ IND (Oct. 28), vs. NYK (Oct. 30), @ CHA (Oct. 31), vs. CHI (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 8.8. The Sixers averaged 8.8 offensive rebounds per game. As the Sixers struggled to rebound in the preseason, coach Nick Nurse wasn't concerned. "We're going to be a good rebounding team," he said then. The Sixers still aren't, ranking 29th in the NBA in offensive rebounding per game and 26th in total rebounds per game. The struggles make some sense as the Sixers front court has been decimated with injury, but it remains concerning and something Nurse is hoping they fix quickly. "I think that our guys understand that we gotta do a better job," he said. -- Kris Rhim

6. Los Angeles Lakers

2026-27 record: 3-1
Previous ranking: 11
Next games: @ LAC (Oct. 28), @ GS (Oct. 30), vs. TOR (Nov. 1), vs. MIA (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 60/60/90. Austin Reaves got off to an unbelievably hot start through the Lakers' 3-0 showing out of the gates, averaging a career-best 26.7 points on 63.9% from the field, 61.5% from 3 and 89.7% from the free throw line entering Tuesday's game. He and Luka Doncic (34.3 points per game) are the only pair of teammates in the top 10 in scoring in the league. They would be even more effective if they took care of the ball better. They also both rank in the top 10 in turnovers per game through three games, with 7.0 for Doncic and 4.3 for Reaves. -- Dave McMenamin

7. Toronto Raptors

2026-27 record: 2-1
Previous ranking: 12
Next games: vs. ORL (Oct. 28), vs. ORL (Oct. 30), @ LAL (Nov. 1), @ LAC (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 0-12. The Raptors' only loss this season came with Leonard sidelined, but Toronto will be without Leonard for a period of weeks as he manages left knee soreness. The concerning part about life without Leonard is that in the Raptors' first look without him, Scottie Barnes had one of the worst outings of his career, finishing 0-12 with three turnovers and a team-worst minus-27 in the 117-94 loss. -- Rhim

8. Boston Celtics

2026-27 record: 3-1
Previous ranking: 6
Next games: vs. CHI (Oct. 30), @ ORL (Nov. 1), @ HOU (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: Jordan Walsh is in the starting lineup. Starting Walsh, a rotational player who started 25 games last season, came as a bit of a surprise with veterans like Sam Hauser and Payton Pritchard on the roster. But so far, Walsh's defense has buoyed the Celtics early in the season, slowing down guards including the Knicks' Jalen Brunson (2-for-7, 5 points against Walsh) and the Pistons' Cade Cunningham (1-for-3, 3 points against Walsh), according to NBA.com. -- Rhim

9. San Antonio Spurs

2026-27 record: 2-2
Previous ranking: 2
Next games: @ UTAH (Oct. 28), vs. MIN (Oct. 31), vs. UTAH (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 1-2 start. The Spurs ran into the combustible mixture of growing pains in trying to evolve their offense with a new starting five while facing two of the West's toughest teams -- Oklahoma City and Houston -- to start the season. So, the early struggles weren't unexpected, and the Spurs are comfortable with taking their lumps early. But in the process of trying to raise its ceiling, San Antonio lowered its floor, a disturbing early trend. Spurs coach Mitch Johnson said, "We've got to just keep getting back to the standard we know we are capable of. Our floor right now is way too low." -- Wright

10. Portland Trail Blazers

2026-27 record: 3-0
Previous ranking: 17
Next games: vs. MEM (Oct. 29), @ UTAH (Oct. 31), @ DEN (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 21-0 start. The Blazers enjoyed the perfect start to the intriguing Damian Lillard and Ja Morant partnership thanks to a blowout win over the Suns in their season opener. Portland raced out to a 21-0 lead in front of a raucous Moda Center crowd that eagerly welcomed Lillard back from an Achilles injury. Though Morant opened the season as a starter, he's had to make great sacrifices to fit into Portland's crowded backcourt rotation. The two-time All-Star is tracking towards career lows in minutes, points, shots and usage rate. -- Golliver

11. Indiana Pacers

2026-27 record: 2-2
Previous ranking: 13
Next games: vs. PHI (Oct. 28), @ MIA (Oct. 30), vs. BKN (Nov. 1), vs. ATL (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 21.8. The number of points Tyrese Haliburton is averaging through his first four games back from injury. He's scored at least 20 in three of the first four games of a season for only the second time in his career, played in a back-to-back this week and he's averaging 9.5 assists. Any worries about him needing to ease back into action have been unfounded. Haliburton looks like his old self after missing 16 months, but the Pacers are going to need to get healthier around him (Ivica Zubac has a sprained left ankle, T.J. McConnell has yet to play in a game in either preseason or regular season and Ben Sheppard tore his meniscus). -- Jamal Collier

12. Denver Nuggets

2026-27 record: 1-2
Previous ranking: 8
Next games: @ NO (Oct. 28), @ PHX (Oct. 30), vs. POR (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: The Nuggets' 119.3 defensive rating is fifth worst in the league. It's been a strange first homestand for the Nuggets. They fell 23 points to the Pelicans and even received some boos, but then stormed back for an overtime win with help from rookie Trevon Brazile, who made a handful of spectacular plays and looks like a second-round steal at a time Denver desperately needs depth. After the game, Nikola Jokic called out the jeering fans, saying they weren't welcome back, and doubled down a couple nights later after they were blown out at home by the previously winless Warriors. -- Anthony Slater

13. Cleveland Cavaliers

2026-27 record: 2-1
Previous ranking: 9
Next games: vs. WAS (Oct. 28), @ ATL (Oct. 29), @ MIL (Oct. 31), vs. OKC (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: Keep an eye on the wing trio of Peyton Watson, Sam Merrill and Jaylon Tyson and how they complement Cleveland's core four throughout the season. That trio has made just 19.5% of their combined 3-pointers so far -- but it's still very early, so there's plenty of time for those role players to turn it around and start making more shots in support of the stars. -- Zach Kram

14. Memphis Grizzlies

2026-27 record: 4-0
Previous ranking: 24
Next games: @ POR (Oct. 29), vs. SAC (Oct. 31), vs. NO (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: Ty Jerome's hot start and the Grizzlies 4-0 start. Memphis' 4-0 start ranks as the second-best in franchise history behind the 2014-15 campaign in which the Grizzlies won their first six games. Perhaps the most eye-popping early trend comes from the way this young team has performed in clutch time. Three of Memphis' first four outings turned out to be clutch time games, with the Grizzlies winning all of them to tie the 76ers for the most clutch wins so far this season. Jerome ranks third in the league in scoring (29.8 points per game) after a career-high 45-point season opener, which he then followed with 31 points against the Kings. -- Wright

15. Atlanta Hawks

2026-27 record: 2-2
Previous ranking: 15
Next games: vs. MIA (Oct. 28), vs. CLE (Oct. 29), @ NO (Oct. 31), @ IND (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: Can Quin Snyder continue to rely heavily on his rotation? One storyline entering the season was whether the Hawks' frontcourt could succeed against quality opponents. The loss at Houston proved they have a long way to go. In the ten-point loss, Atlanta was outrebounded 40-22 on the offensive glass (52-35 overall) and were minus-11 in free-throw attempts. The lone frontcourt player with a positive plus-minus was Onyeka Okongwu. Through the first four games, nine players have averaged more than 18 MPG, with only starter Jalen Johnson averaging more than 30 MPG. -- Bobby Marks

16. New York Knicks

2026-27 record: 1-3
Previous ranking: 3
Next games: @ CHI (Oct. 28), @ PHI (Oct. 30), vs. BKN (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 30th. That's what the Knicks ranked at in both offensive efficiency and raw scoring entering Tuesday's game. It's a small sample size, but the Knicks have barely shown more than flashes of that potent offense. "We get a little comfortable," Jalen Brunson said after Sunday's loss to Orlando, in which New York gave up 40 fourth-quarter points to the Magic. Before Tuesday, Mikal Bridges registered donuts at the foul line and 3-point line. One is expected, the other is not.-- Goodwill

17. Charlotte Hornets

2026-27 record: 3-1
Previous ranking: 23
Next games: @ DET (Oct. 28), @ WAS (Oct. 30), vs. PHI (Oct. 31), vs. DET (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 36.3 PPG. New Hornets Grayson Allen and Naz Reid came to Charlotte in trades for Miles Bridges and Ball, respectively, and both sharpshooters are excelling in their new digs. Allen and Reid have combined to average 36.3 points per game while making 44% of their 3-pointers, and both players rank in the top 10 in the NBA in made 3s. -- Kram

18. Washington Wizards

2026-27 record: 2-2
Previous ranking: 22
Next games: @ CLE (Oct. 28), vs. CHA (Oct. 30), @ ORL (Nov. 2

Most surprising stat or trend: 8.8 PPG. After averaging 16.3 points per game with a 26% usage rate in a promising sophomore season, Alex Sarr is down to 8.8 PPG with a 14% usage rate this year. That decline epitomizes the difficult balancing act for the Wizards as they try to win games with veteran stars Trae Young and Anthony Davis, while also providing opportunities for their many prospects to develop on the court. -- Kram

19. Phoenix Suns

2026-27 record: 1-2
Previous ranking: 18
Next games: vs. DEN (Oct. 30), @ GS (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 40. Devin Booker recorded the 40th 40-point game of his career with 43 points on 17-for-25 shooting in the Suns' 131-122 win over the Warriors opening week. It's the most in franchise history, with Amare Stoudemire trailing significantly behind at No. 2 with 15 of them. Phoenix is off to a slow start, however, with Booker combining for just 26 points on 8-for-20 shooting in the Suns' other two losses. -- McMenamin

20. Orlando Magic

2026-27 record: 1-2
Previous ranking: 16
Next games: @ TOR (Oct. 28), @ TOR (Oct. 30), vs. BOS (Nov. 1), vs. WAS (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 3. Injuries are forcing Orlando to utilize its third starting lineup in four games when it plays Toronto on Wednesday. Former All-Star Paolo Banchero is out indefinitely with an ankle injury, while Jalen Suggs will miss at least two weeks due to a bone bruise in his right knee. Injuries have impacted them in the last two seasons, with Banchero and Franz Wagner playing only 64 games together in that span. -- Marks

21. Utah Jazz

2026-27 record: 1-3
Previous ranking: 20
Next games: vs. SA (Oct. 28), vs. POR (Oct. 31), @ SA (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: Ace Bailey stepping up during early Jazz injuries. Utah's frontcourt has been ravaged by injuries, as Jaren Jackson Jr. (knee), Lauri Markkanen (wrist) and Jusuf Nurkic (toe) are all sidelined. Second-year forward Bailey's performance has been a silver lining during the Jazz's rough start. Bailey, the No. 5 pick in last year's draft, has back-to-back double-doubles, averaging 17 points, 11 rebounds, 3.5 assists and two blocks in the two games. -- MacMahon

22. Dallas Mavericks

2026-27 record: 2-2
Previous ranking: 21
Next games: vs. OKC (Oct. 28), vs. HOU (Oct. 30), vs. SAC (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: Cooper Flagg's disruptive abilities. Flagg's disruptive defensive tendencies were as much of a factor as his offensive potential in scouts and executives considering him one of the best draft prospects in a generation and those skills have been on display early this season. Flagg leads the league with 3.7 steals per game and ranks in the top 20 in blocks (1.7). He had five steals and three blocks during his 29-point, 11-assist masterpiece in Monday's win in Miami. The only other teens to ever record at least five steals and three blocks in a game: Kevin Garnett and Wembanyama, both of whom went on to win a Defensive Player of the Year award. -- MacMahon

23. LA Clippers

2026-27 record: 1-2
Previous ranking: 27
Next games: vs. LAL (Oct. 28), @ MIN (Oct. 30), @ GS (Nov. 1), vs. TOR (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 26.3%. That is Rui Hachimura's field goal percentage through his first three games with the Clippers after signing a two-year, $28 million contract to move from Crypto.com Arena to the Intuit Dome in the offseason. The dip in efficiency comes off a season when he shot 51.4% for the Lakers -- the second-best clip of his career -- and raised his level to 54.9% in the playoffs. Hachimura only had 11 games last season out of the 68 he played where he shot under 30% for the game. He's done that in two out of his first three games with the Clippers. -- McMenamin

24. Miami Heat

2026-27 record: 0-4
Previous ranking: 14
Next games: @ ATL (Oct. 28), vs. IND (Oct. 30), @ LAL (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 105.3. We won't compare this current iteration of the Heat to Miami's inaugural team in 1988-89, which lost 17 straight games. But like their first team, the current roster is only the second team in franchise history to start the season with four straight losses. The lack of success derives from an offensive rating that ranks 27th (105.3) and a defensive rating that sits at 24th (118.8). One trend to watch is whether Miami can improve from the perimeter. The Heat rank 25th in three-point percentage and have no player besides Portis Jr. and Davion Mitchell shooting greater than 35%. -- Marks

25. Chicago Bulls

2026-27 record: 1-3
Previous ranking: 26
Next games: vs. NYK (Oct. 28), @ BOS (Oct. 30), @ PHI (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 25.5. That's the number of minutes Josh Giddey is averaging per game in what has been an underwhelming start to the season. On opening night, Giddey revealed he injured his left wrist and will have to manage the injury all season. Both his production -- 7.0 points and 7.3 assists on 33% shooting -- and playing time have dipped as a result, and the Bulls offense has sputtered out of the gates. Entering Tuesday, they had the worst offensive rating in the league through four games. -- Collier

26. New Orleans Pelicans

2026-27 record: 0-3
Previous ranking: 25
Next games: vs. DEN (Oct. 28), vs. SAC (Oct. 29), vs. ATL (Oct. 31), @ MEM (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: 23-point collapse. Jamahl Mosley is still seeking his first win as coach after New Orleans inexplicably blew a 23-point lead to Denver on Saturday. The Pelicans might regret their stumbles out of the gate: The NBA handed them a soft early-season schedule, playing nine of their first 13 games against teams that missed the 2026 playoffs. Mosley has started 2025 lottery pick Jeremiah Fears, but the guard's abysmal shooting -- 29% from the field and 18.2% from deep -- has been a real drag on the Pelicans' offense. -- Golliver

27. Golden State Warriors

2026-27 record: 1-3
Previous ranking: 19
Next games: @ MIN (Oct. 28), vs. LAL (Oct. 30), vs. LAC (Nov. 1), vs. PHX (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: It couldn't have been a louder opening week to a career for Yaxel Lendeborg. After getting in a public dust-up with Doncic (they face each other again on Friday), the rookie wing went on a statistical binge, becoming the fourth player since 1986 to compile at least 85 points and 35 rebounds in his first four games. Shaquille O'Neal, Patrick Ewing and David Robinson are the other three. It didn't take long for him to earn Steve Kerr's trust. Lendeborg put away the Nuggets on Monday night with Stephen Curry on the bench and Kerr said afterward, "He's going to be a guy who closes games." -- Slater

28. Milwaukee Bucks

2026-27 record: 1-3
Previous ranking: 29
Next games: vs. HOU (Oct. 28), vs. CLE (Oct. 31), @ MIN (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: Zero. That's the number of minutes Gary Trent Jr. has played for the Bucks this season despite signing a four-year, $64 million contract during the offseason. The deal confused several team executives around the league when it was agreed upon, and those questions have only increased as Trent -- the fourth-highest-paid player on the roster -- can't even crack the rotation. At least Milwaukee has avoided having a zero in the win column after a win against Indiana on Monday, dodging what would have been the Bucks' first 0-4 start in 50 years. -- Collier

29. Brooklyn Nets

2026-27 record: 0-4
Previous ranking: 28
Next games: vs. DET (Oct. 30), @ IND (Nov. 1), @ NYK (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: Julius Randle has been efficient, despite the losses. If there was any notion that Randle would be a selfish star coming into a Nets team stuck at the bottom of the standings, it's been anything but. He kept them in their first two games -- which were respectable losses to Charlotte and Cleveland -- and led them to an overtime loss against the Celtics on Tuesday night. He leads the Nets in scoring (22.0), rebounding (7.0) and assists (6.3) while shooting over 50% from the field and 45% from 3. For a team that will struggle to score all season, having Randle aggressive will at least keep this young team in games. -- Goodwill

30. Sacramento Kings

2026-27 record: 0-4
Previous ranking: 30
Next games: @ NO (Oct. 29), @ MEM (Oct. 31), @ DAL (Nov. 2)

Most surprising stat or trend: As expected, rookie guard Darius Acuff Jr. has received the greenest of lights. He attempted 24, 26 and 23 shots in his first three games, surpassing Durant for the most shots three games into a career in the modern era. But the Kings received concerning news regarding their other wing asset, as small forward Keegan Murray will miss at least the next two weeks while dealing with stiffness in his surgically repaired left ankle. It's been bothering Murray throughout training camp and he hasn't been moving well to open the season. He is in the first season of a five-year, $140 million extension. -- Slater

stories.headline: NFL Week 8 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips: What we're hearing
stories.summary: Are changes coming for the Jets? Could the Chiefs add at the trade deadline? Will the Colts keep unloading? And what's going on in the AFC North standings?
stories.body:
It's Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season, and we're under two weeks away from the trade deadline. Insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been calling sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

Which teams are most likely to bring in help before the Nov. 10 deadline? Which players are likeliest to end up in a new city? And will the Colts continue dealing away players? Jeremy and Dan have updates on the trade market. Plus, we look into what's happening with the struggling Jets and what's going on in the chaotic AFC North, where the Browns are in first and the Ravens are in last.

It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions, hand out useful fantasy football nuggets and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 8.

Jump to:

Aggressive teams at the deadline

Players likely to move | Colts dealing

Jets changes | AFC North chaos

Fantasy advice

Which team is most likely to be aggressive in acquiring help at the deadline?
Fowler: The Chiefs appear poised to do something at wide receiver. Injuries to Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton have created holes in the passing game that running back Kenneth Walker III can't mask alone. The Chiefs have managed to win games despite those injuries, but Sunday night in Seattle was a reminder of how ugly things can look without adequate downfield playmakers.

Enough receivers will be available in the coming weeks, so the Chiefs can get good value trading for the high-impact players or lower-cost options. The Colts' Josh Downs would be a fit for the Chiefs. The Browns' Jerry Jeudy would also fit, though Cleveland is not inclined to deal him now barring a significant offer.

Graziano: The Chiefs always seem to do something at wide receiver at the deadline. Usually it's a smaller move such as Kadarius Toney or late-career DeAndre Hopkins, but the team has a history of targeted trade-deadline additions at the position. I expect Kansas City to be active in trying to add a player or two to boost the offense, be that another pass catcher, an offensive lineman or both.

The teams that are most interesting to me are the surprises. Would the first-place Giants believe they're in position to trade a draft pick or two for a win-now player? Would the AFC North-leading Browns feel compelled to reward their current roster for its surprising first-half success by adding a player who can help take them to the next level? We saw the Colts do this last year with the big swing for Sauce Gardner.

Of course, last year's Colts are proof that this approach doesn't always work, but what do you think? Would the Browns veer from their long-term building plans to try to make a 2026 run with Deshaun Watson at QB?

Fowler: Cleveland is a low-key team to watch at the deadline. The Browns are 5-2 and like to make deals. Defensive line help will be available if they tap into it. And adding a versatile blocker, either at tight end or H-back, would be timely, perhaps providing a player similar to what Todd Monken had in Baltimore with Patrick Ricard.

Seattle has already made a move with the deal for Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson. Edge rusher and running back are positions Seahawks GM John Schneider could monitor, as well.

Graziano: Yeah, Tuesday was a big day in the NFC West arms race. It makes me wonder what the Rams are thinking. They obviously made their big moves in the offseason, but things haven't worked, and everyone's favorite superteam has fallen behind the 49ers and Seahawks in the division. I wonder whether there's another move for the Rams to make -- they could use a speedy wide receiver if one is available -- and whether they still have the draft picks and/or desire to add more to a roster that was already supposed to be loaded.

I'm also very curious to see what the Jaguars do. They see themselves as a top AFC contender. I agree with them, but they could use one more piece up front on defense. Remember, the Jags were kind of a surprise at last year's deadline with their move for Jakobi Meyers, who helped fuel their second-half run.

Which player are you most confident will get traded somewhere before the deadline?
Fowler: Let's go with Jaguars receiver Brian Thomas Jr. Several execs I've spoken to believe Thomas' days in Jacksonville are numbered due to his diminished role in Year 3. He has trade value, and the Jaguars would be smart to explore that option. One potential deterrent: Jacksonville is in a winning window and needs all hands on deck for the stretch run. Thomas, at worst, still commands defensive coverage, but he hasn't caught a pass in the past two games and was essentially benched in London in Week 6.

None of the top trade options around the league is a slam dunk to happen, but place Thomas in the Marvin Harrison Jr. category of a receiver badly needing a fresh start. The safer bet might end up being Vikings wide receiver Jauan Jennings, who isn't a primary option in that offense and is also a trade candidate.

Graziano: Thomas is my answer, too. He clearly hasn't been a big part of Jacksonville's offense since coach Liam Coen arrived last season. Thomas would surely prefer to either be a bigger part of the Jaguars' offense or go to a team where he can have a sizable role. And there are plenty of teams around the league that still view him as a high-end talent at a premium position and would give up something of value to get him.

Like you said, this closely mirrors the Harrison situation. Thomas is two months younger than Harrison, was also drafted in the first round in 2024 and showed enough promise as a rookie that there's reason to believe a change of scenery could bring out the best in him. Thomas hasn't made any public noise about wanting out, but neither did Harrison. Still, Harrison and his agents were able to work with the Cardinals behind the scenes to find a solution that made everyone happy. I expect the same thing to happen for Thomas.

Going back to your Jennings mention, I agree that the most likely guys to be traded are the slightly lower-profile names if simply because they won't cost as much to add. But I also imagine Cardinals edge rusher Josh Sweat will be of interest to teams needing defensive help over the next couple of weeks.

Fowler: Yeah, Dan, Sweat certainly fits the profile of a prime trade candidate, and some around the league have linked the Cowboys to his services.

What about the Colts? Are more moves coming after they dealt Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner?
Graziano: With the Colts tearing things down, veteran wideouts such as Keenan Allen and Laquon Treadwell might have appeal as depth players on contenders that need help at receiver. Defensive tackle Grover Stewart and wide receiver Josh Downs are also on expiring contracts and didn't get extensions this offseason.

The guy who did get an extension, running back Jonathan Taylor, might be the most interesting of the bunch. Even after his recent extension, Taylor has a tradeable contract. The Colts would have to absorb $10 million in dead money next year, and the acquiring team would have to take on whatever prorated portion of Taylor's $8 million salary plus bonus compensation is left for this season. He's scheduled to make $16.02 million next year, and right now that's not guaranteed, though it converts to a full guarantee five days after the Super Bowl.

So technically, you could acquire Taylor without any commitment beyond this season, but you'd also retain the ability to keep him past 2026 if you are comfortable with that price. I believe Tennessee's Tony Pollard is the more likely running back to be dealt, ahead of Taylor or Saquon Barkley, but if the Colts are in full rebuilding mode, you can't rule anything out.

Fowler: Talks are heating up quickly. Nelson had interest from several suitors before going to the Seahawks, including the Packers, thus expediting his market. Assistant GM Ed Dodds' phone will be lighting up this week. Buckner was also a player people were watching before he was dealt to the 49ers on Tuesday.

Downs has emerged as a hot name this week because multiple teams looking for receiver help have shown interest. But the Colts are thin at receiver already, so trading Downs would severely limit the offense, though my sense is he would not be against a change of scenery. And as multiple people around the league pointed out Tuesday, trading Taylor isn't a slam dunk because unlike Buckner and Nelson, he is not an impending free agent. He will also be a boon for whoever is coaching the Colts in 2027, be it current head man Shane Steichen or an outside hire.

How long until we see changes for the Jets?
Graziano: Most people I talk to think Aaron Glenn will get to coach through the end of this season before the team evaluates the two-year sample and decides whether to bring him back for a third. The caveats are that owners are unpredictable and that this particular owner fired his last head coach relatively early in the 2024 season. Glenn has some things going for him that Robert Saleh didn't, mainly his connection with the franchise from his time as a Jets player. Ownership likes Glenn and wants to be proved right about him being a good head coach.

That said, he has struggled with a few tasks specific to head coaches, most prominently end-of-half clock management. And his choice of Frank Reich as offensive coordinator after one year of Tanner Engstrand is coming under criticism as the offense struggles to score points. A defensive head coach is often done in by his inability to find the right offensive coordinator, so unless the Jets get things turned around on offense by the end of this season, that could be a detrimental data point for Glenn's chances to stick around.

Fowler: My sense after asking around to those in the industry who closely follow such things is that Glenn likely will get some time to attempt to right the ship, but the hot seat conversation is real, and this job is on the radar for potential change at some point. It's important to note that the Jets were not viewed as a playoff-caliber team in the offseason or preseason. They're a young team in transition, and they're right to expect modest progress. On that front, they look more competitive and more capable, but they're still 2-5, which sort of offsets those first two points.

Glenn can lift his standing in two areas: better game management/situational football and maximizing the playmakers on offense with improved overall play. This stat from ESPN Jets reporter Rich Cimini is shocking: The Jets have been outscored 107-6 in the final two minutes of the second quarter under Glenn. Glenn must prove that he can manage the clock better at the end of halves. And this offense should rank better than 27th in the NFL given its talent level. Garrett Wilson is already frustrated -- again.

Graziano: And that's not good. One reason the Jets moved on from Aaron Rodgers after the 2024 season was concern over his relationship with Wilson and their belief that they had to make sure the wideout was happy and wanted to be there long term.

So here's the way I see it with the Jets. Glenn doesn't have to make the playoffs this season to keep his job and never did. But this is a team with three first-round picks in April and a plan to somehow, some way, finally find its long-term franchise quarterback. What the Jets want to have established by the end of this season is at least a foundation of a winning culture and an environment in which a young quarterback would be in position to quickly thrive and be happy. It's hard to look at the Jets right now and think they're on either one of those tracks. There is time to turn it around, but if it keeps going the way it has so far, this is absolutely a situation we'll be watching for a potential change.

Fowler: I also suspect that any major changes would be limited to the coaching staff. General manager Darren Mougey is ascending and has acquitted himself well through the past two years. His trades have New York positioned for three top-12 picks in April's draft as it currently stands. The roster is improved. Whoever the head coach is in 2027 will be in a good situation ... on paper. Ownership is viewed as a hurdle in some league circles, though it sounds like Woody Johnson wants to change that narrative and could be patient with Glenn as a result.

Browns in first? Ravens in last? What are you hearing on the upside-down AFC North?
Fowler: That the Browns are no fluke. I'm not ready to crown them the division winners, but they are well-stocked with young talent. Deshaun Watson has rediscovered (at least some of) his old form, and the schedule is soft. Cleveland has faced three teams with losing records, and three of its next four opponents are also below .500. It's at least a good enough schedule to keep things interesting.

The Steelers aren't lighting it up offensively but are creating an identity with star running back Jaylen Warren and heavy personnel (two tight ends or six offensive linemen). Pittsburgh seems to be in a similar spot to where it was in recent seasons -- good enough to win nine or 10 games and sneak into the playoffs but lacking juice beyond that. But what it's doing with heavier packages, including two-tight-end sets, has me intrigued. And don't discount the Steelers improving their roster at the deadline. Either way, this is shaping up to be the most balanced division in football.

Graziano: I don't believe the Browns or Steelers are as good as their records indicate. I mean, Watson is 27th in the league in QBR, and Cleveland has allowed 13 more points than it has scored. This is a mirage, along with some really good coaching by Todd Monken. And the Steelers just keep eking out these grueling wins against mediocre competition and looking a lot like they did for the past half-decade of the Mike Tomlin era.

Moving to Cincinnati, the Bengals have the one clearly elite unit in the AFC North, and it's the offense that hung 35 points on the Ravens in the second half Sunday. Cincinnati's defense is also playing at a higher level than we're used to. Based on what we've seen (and yes, I watched the Bengals lose in Pittsburgh with my own eyes thanks to two horrible mistakes on punt plays), I have them as the class of this division, and I believe that's how it will play out in the end. Sunday was a statement game for Cincinnati, and the statement is, "We are better than you are."

Fowler: The Bengals might be the most dangerous. We knew going into the season that they needed just passable defense; Joe Burrow and his side of the ball could handle the rest. That lopsided win in Baltimore on Sunday was a statement on both accounts. Cincinnati is convincing as a whole, but its ground game remains concerning. Last year's rushing attack ranked 29th in the league, and after hoping for improvement, this season's group ranks ... 30th. Teams that rank near the bottom in rushing typically don't make the playoffs. Burrow can overcome this issue at times, but that's hard to do over 17 games.

So while I mostly agree with you on Cincinnati's interdivision potential, I'm taking Baltimore for the division if Lamar Jackson is back this week and for the duration of the season. Here's to expecting Baltimore to tighten up and prove the Cincinnati game was an aberration.

Where are you at with the Ravens, Dan? History tells us that a hobbled Jackson equates to eight- or nine-win seasons for Baltimore. But the team's ceiling remains high.

Graziano: That seems to be the consensus opinion and has been since the offseason -- that Baltimore has a strong roster and should be a top AFC contender when everyone's healthy. But I have concerns.

The Ravens definitely need Jackson back as soon and as healthy as possible. This isn't graduate-level NFL analysis. He is as big a difference-maker as there is in the league. The Ravens can get by without him, but they cannot excel in that state -- and excel is what they're going to have to do to win this division (even if I'm not with you yet on the level of excellence being displayed by the two teams atop the AFC North right now). The big problem the Ravens have is that the two games they've lost without Jackson are to the Browns and Bengals, both of whom are ahead of them in the division and now have a tiebreaker edge as well.

Jackson's health isn't the only issue. Derrick Henry looks a step slow for the first time and is getting stuffed at a high rate in short-yardage situations. The defense's disappearance in the second half Sunday must sound some alarm bells, doesn't it? Wasn't this supposed to be the Trey Hendrickson revenge game? The new coaching staff is unproven and hasn't had to manage a team through the inevitable ups and downs of a season. I believe Jesse Minter is a good coach who can do it, but we have not seen whether he can or will. We don't really know what the current, post-Harbaugh version of the Ravens is or how it will hold up as the season goes along.

What is your best piece of fantasy football advice for this week?
Graziano: After the week I just had in fantasy, my best advice is to not ask me for advice. But since you're insisting ... try to trade for Seahawks RB Jadarian Price. He's back at practice this week after missing the past four games while on injured reserve with a chest injury. I have no idea whether he'll play this week or how much, but he'll be back at some point soon. He was their first-round pick this year, and they just traded for Nelson, a move that will help their run game immensely.

Yes, Zach Charbonnet is close to returning, but he's also Zach Charbonnet, not Bijan Robinson. At best, the Seahawks will use Charbonnet the way they always have, which leaves room for someone else to produce at a high level. Price has had fumble issues and rookie growing pains, but the Seahawks drafted him because they saw him as a ready-made prospect who could help this season. Given how much Nelson can improve the run game, that Seattle's remaining schedule is friendly for fantasy running backs and that Price is probably sitting in someone's IR spot in your league, you might be able to get a steal.

Fowler: Grab insurance plays at RB such as the Colts' Seth McGowan. This is the time of year when RB depth thins due to injury. The Colts' trade plans could result in a deal for Jonathan Taylor, which would open up the backfield for McGowan. Even if they don't trade Taylor, McGowan is probably worth the roster spot if you have one to spare. The Titans' Tyjae Spears is also tempting if Tennessee gets a great offer for Tony Pollard.

stories.headline: Lineups, live updates from Brewers-Rays World Series Game 5
stories.summary: After a dramatic Game 4, the Fall Classic continues tonight at Tropicana Field. Here's the latest.
stories.body:
After a dramatic comeback victory on Tuesday, the Tampa Bay Rays lived to play another day.

The Rays won on a walk-off single by Ben Williamson on Tuesday, denying the Milwaukee Brewers their first World Series title -- for now.

With Milwaukee up 3-1 in the series, will the Brewers raise the trophy on their second chance? Or will the Rays keep their postseason alive and push this series back to Milwaukee? And who is available to pitch for each team after Tuesday's marathon?

Stay tuned for pregame lineups, in-game action and postgame takeaways.

Key links: How to win World Series | Playoff MVP tracker | Full schedule

Milwaukee Brewers at Tampa Bay Rays (8 p.m. ET)
Starting pitchers: Jacob Misiorowski vs. TBD

What Brewers need to do to win: Play a clean game, something they've weirdly had a hard time doing in these playoffs. Brewers infielders have committed eight errors in these playoffs. Two of them occurred in Game 4 and led to runs, both of them errant throws from third base.

The Brewers should feel good about their chances in Game 5. They'll have their ace, Misiorowski, going up against a Rays team with few legitimate pitching options. And they'll be coming off a night in which their hitters produced 12 of the 13 hardest-hit balls with little to show for it. If they don't get in their own way, they'll be in good shape. -- Alden Gonzalez

What Rays must do to extend series: Make Misiorowski work. The Brewers have not relied on the hard-throwing right-hander for a heavy workload in the postseason. In Game 1, the presumptive NL Cy Young Award winner held the Rays to one run over five innings but was pulled after throwing just 78 pitches. He threw 88 pitches across four innings in his first playoff outing in the NLDS against the Padres and 94 pitches over 4⅓ innings in his NLCS start against the Dodgers. After using their best relievers heavily in Game 4, the Brewers could look for more length from Misiorowski in Game 5. They have the clear advantage in the pitching matchup with Tampa Bay likely opting for a bullpen game. It's on Tampa Bay's lineup to erase the edge. -- Jorge Castillo

Who each team has available to pitch

In a nutshell, when you're a manager looking at the middle game of a three-game set and trying to map out your pitching plan for the finale, you don't want to see numbers like these from Game 4:

• Fifteen pitchers used over 23 innings and four hours, 20 minutes

• 367 pitches thrown

• 90 batters faced

If you're Tampa Bay skipper Kevin Cash, you'll take it. You won, so you get to play another one. The expenditure of pitching resources is a little harder to stomach for Milwaukee's Pat Murphy, whose team lost a late lead that could have closed out a championship.

"We drained a lot of pitching, as they did, and that's part of playing a tight ballgame," Murphy said.

Now that the dust has settled from a long, dramatic, season-extending contest, what's left? How does the pitching landscape look after this grinder of a Game 4?

Brewers

Murphy surprised no one after the game in saying that Misiorowski will start Game 5 on Wednesday. Misiorowski started Game 1 on Oct. 23 and so will be pitching on four days rest. He made just four of his 30 starts this season on four days rest but went 1-1 with a 1.64 ERA in those games. Over 22 innings, Misiorowski had 34 strikeouts and three walks in those games. Murphy would take those kind of numbers in Game 5.

Alas, Misiorowski hasn't pitched at that level during the postseason and you have to figure that Murphy will once again need four or five innings from his bullpen. The big question will be how he might bridge the gap between Misiorowski and Trevor Megill or Aaron Ashby in a potential close-out situation.

Megill appeared in Game 4 but faced just one batter and threw five pitches to close out the eighth before giving way to Aaron Ashby. When asked at the podium after the game if he might have gotten more out of Megill, Murphy simply said, "Yes." He will likely need more in Game 5.

Ashby went 2 ⅓ innings but retired all seven batters he faced and threw just 31 pitches, a total he's surpassed 11 times this season. Ashby groused about being removed on Tuesday but since he didn't pitch in Game 3 and, after Game 5, there will either be a travel day or the season will be over, you have to figure Ashby can give Murphy at least an inning.

The same holds true for Abner Uribe, who threw two innings but faced the minimum of six batters, whom he retired on just 19 pitches. He also didn't pitch the Game 3 blowout so should be ready for an inning on Wednesday.

Thus Murphy should have an ideal plan in place: Misiorowski to some progression of Uribe, Ashby and Megill. Whether he needs another reliever or relievers in addition to that will depend on the score and Misiorowski's effectiveness.

Rays

Things are tricker for the Rays even though they used one fewer pitcher than Milwaukee in Game 4. While their top relievers should be OK -- Bryan Baker, Kevin Kelly and Cam Booser all appeared but didn't have to labor through their outings -- the Rays probably can't roll out one of their primary starters and hope he goes deep.

After Game 4, Cash said that the Rays would be looking at their options and that no decision had been made. One obvious possibility would be to start Game 2 starter Drew Rasmussen on short rest. Rasmussen only went 3 ⅔ innings but threw 89 pitches to do it.

If Cash opts to start Rasmussen, it may be for a shorter outing, which would be less than ideal. If Cash can find an alternative to navigate the game while keeping Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta on normal rest, that would be ideal. The big problem there of course is that the Rays have to win Game 4 or that's that.

The monkey wrench in the Rays' plan was that Game 1 starter Nick Martinez came out of the bullpen in Game 4 and worked two innings, throwing 33 pitches. So the Rays' problems start at the outset. Cash will likely opt for some kind of bullpen game, perhaps with Rasmussen in a bulk role, but we'll see.

However the Rays plan it, there are just glad they have a game to plan for. -- Bradford Doolittle

It's a smaller schedule of games for NHL fans on Wednesday, but all four matchups are captivating for one reason or another.

That includes the next matchup in the Battle of Alberta, along with a rematch between the Avalanche and Devils after New Jersey's 4-3 win on Oct. 20.

Here's a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details:

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Philadelphia Flyers at Washington Capitals

7:30 p.m. ET (TNT) | WSH -238, O/U: 6.5

With this being the final season of Alex Ovechkin's record-breaking NHL career, he gets to play against all of his Metro Division rivals four times each. This will be the first showdown against the Flyers, with the rest coming Nov. 25, Apr. 1 and Apr. 10.

For his career, Ovechkin has 54 goals and 32 assists in 82 career regular-season games against Philly, including two tallies in the most recent matchup this past March 31.

The two teams split their season series in 2025-26, and the Flyers would appear to need the two points on the line quite a bit more given their lackluster start.

Calgary Flames at Edmonton Oilers

8:30 p.m. ET (ESPN) | EDM -218, O/U: 6.5

No matter the players involved, there is always a little extra juice when the NHL's two Alberta-based teams square off. That's no different this season, despite the fact that the Flames haven't made the postseason since 2022 -- when the Oilers knocked them out in five games in the second round.

This will be the first matchup between the clubs this season, and it will (likely) feature the NHL's second star of the week, Devin Cooley, in goal for the Flames.

On the other side, the Oilers have the NHL's first star of the week, Leon Draisaitl, who hopes to get the upper hand in this matchup. He'll have help; while Drasaitl is second in the NHL in scoring this season, with 24 points through 12 games, teammate Connor McDavid is first, with 34 points in the same span.

New Jersey Devils at Colorado Avalanche

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | COL -192, O/U: 6.5

Just 25 hours after opening puck drop against the Central Division powerhouse Dallas Stars, the Devils will face off against the Central Division powerhouse Colorado Avalanche.

In the teams' first matchup this season, the Devils got out to a 3-1 lead early in the third period, and Jesper Boqvist put a puck into the empty net at 16:05. The Avs got two back -- both credited to Artturi Lehkonen -- but couldn't find the equalizer.

Will Wednesday's game include as exciting of a finish?

Toronto Maple Leafs at Seattle Kraken

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | TOR -115, O/U: 6.5

It's still quite early in the season, but both of these teams enter this contest in playoff positions in their respective divisions after missing out on the postseason fun in 2026.

The Leafs will hope they get an effort like the one they had Saturday in Edmonton (a 7-2 win) as opposed to Monday in Calgary (a 5-2 loss). Seattle has also had some inconsistent results as of late, with wins over the Mammoth and Red Wings sandwiched between blowout losses to the Panthers and Wild.

stories.headline: Arteta, Alonso, Iraola: Three Premier League managers all come from one tiny club
stories.summary: Whether it be the Premier League, Champions League or World Cup, hiring a coach from Spain's northern coast is bringing clubs guaranteed success.
stories.body:
There is irresistible evidence right now that signing coaching talent from Spain's northern coast brings guaranteed success, and Arsenal, Liverpool, Aston Villa and Chelsea need no convincing.

In international terms, the European and world champions (Spain) are coached by a Basque (Luis De La Fuente), in club terms, double Champions League winners PSG dance to the tune of another north-coast Spaniard, Luis Enrique, and the reigning Europa League holders and English champions owe their success to a couple of guys, Unai Emery and Mikel Arteta, who grew up within a few miles of one another in San Sebastián (part of the Gipuzkoa territory in Spain's Basque country).

It is, literally, a phenomenon. This is a coaching domination by a small community on a grand scale.

Now the fascinating prospect is that four of England's great clubs will all be jostling for trophies and bragging rights this season, in the Premier League and in Europe, under the control of coaches who all learned at one amateur Gipuzkoa football club on the Bay of Biscay coastline.

Arteta, Emery, Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso have already enjoyed jaw-dropping coaching success -- historic triumphs with Arsenal, Bournemouth, Bayer Leverkusen, Sevilla and Aston Villa between them. Now, they will all be going toe-to-toe for England's silverware.

What they also share, particularly Arteta, Iraola and Alonso, is an identical development path, often criss-crossing experiences in their home town of San Sebastián, being trained under the same ethos, often by the same coaches.

The amateur club in question is Antiguoko, which can claim partial responsibility for Bournemouth earning their first ever UEFA qualification (Iraola played for Antiguoko as a kid then, eventually, began his coaching career there), for Bayer Leverkusen winning their only Bundesliga title (Alonso) and for Arteta bringing Arsenal their first Premier League trophy in 22 years. Remarkable, right?

Those who run football at Antiguoko, and around the Gipuzkoa region, are beginning to smile with resignation as Europe's media approach them and demand the magic formula which has produced these brilliant alumni (and a host of other key figures in coaching and directorial roles around the continent).

There's no magic -- just ideology, hard work, decades of development and attention to detail.

Iraola says: "The number of successful coaches formed in the Basque Country receives a lot of attention because, despite being a small place, we have a great football culture."

When Arteta was last asked about what it is that makes Basque coaches so successful he gave a simple, short answer: "It's about passion we have and the education that we all got."

That education includes the fact that kids who follow the Arteta-Alonso-Iraola route in Gipuzkoa, aren't allowed to belong to a single club, practising a single sport, until they're 10 years or older.

The idea being that young boys and girls must continue to learn and develop through other sports like basketball, handball and volleyball before they, eventually, specialise.

The concept is to keep mixing with differently talented youngsters, to keep working on different spacial and athletic disciplines, to learn from and then cross-fertilise eclectic ideas.

Written down in black and white it makes simple sense, doesn't it?

There is also a huge emphasis placed on the coaches who train kids earning good qualifications, having a shared ideology, and being given respect by the community around them.

Again, doesn't that sound like basic common sense and decency?

During research for this column, Manu Diaz, the president of the Guipúzcoa Football Federation, explained: "There's a disproportionate number of coaches in our region because of our sense of community -- people want to give something back.

"Kids want to become coaches, they wait for their 16th birthday to be able to start doing their badges as if they were waiting for the chance to learn to drive. You also learn from a young age how to be part of a big group and that lends itself to eventually being good at leading. The coach is very well respected.

"People can invent a narrative that there is a common school of football here but really more than a shared way of seeing the game, it's a shared way of seeing life. There's a Basque word that sums it up: 'Auzolan' which refers to working together with neighbourly cooperation."

Some of that is evidenced by the way in which Arteta, Alonso, Iraola and co. learned their earliest football skills, and learned "neighbourly cooperation" via the phenomenon particular to San Sebastián where huge numbers of junior football matches are played on the two main beaches.

When the tide is out, parents, kids and coaches literally draw out a series of pitches on the flat, hard La Concha and Ondarreta sand, drag out stored goal-frames and play dozens of matches until the Cantabrian sea sweeps in again.

The pitch-lines need to be scraped out by hand in the sand. Speed and teamwork is of the essence -- not just when the matches start but in joining together to create the massive jigsaw of 10, 12, or 15 pitches as quickly as possible so that a host of games, with boys and girls of all ages, can take place. Teamwork makes the dream work.

Alonso, who won his first-ever trophy with Arteta in a tournament with Antiguoko when the pair were barely in their teens, explains: "I was lucky enough to have Mikel, who was also crazy about football, in our neighbourhood. Every day we'd go down to the beach on our skateboards to play tennis, surf, and, of course, play football."

There's no getting away from the fact that the Basque school of football development uses phrases and ideology which the modern, money-obsessed, fast-paced, hard-nosed elite world of football would find hokey and old-fashioned.

Perhaps that's the key: All the things that drive old-school fans crazy, that make them feel detached from the modern, foreign-owned, exorbitantly priced, corporate and investment-fund football are the opposite to the Antiguoko, Gipuzkoa, Basque ways which gave us Alonso, Arteta, Iraola and Emery.

"It shines a spotlight on one of European football's premier youth academies," an Antiguoko spokesperson told ESPN. "We are a neighbourhood institution -- modest in resources yet colossal in influence. We have served for decades as a true school for both footballing and human development.

"These guys who now work in the Premier League have publicly acknowledged the profound impact Antiguoko K.E. had on their athletic and personal development. We nurture players, by fostering raw talent, but also via a culture of hard work, tactical intelligence, game interpretation, and collective commitment.

"A footballing philosophy grounded in competitiveness and holistic development. Our club embodies the very essence of local grassroots football. Here, football is in the air from a very young age -- but so, too, are discipline, a sense of closeness, and a deep feeling of belonging."

Five years ago Alonso was one of the co-authors of the Real Sociedad training manual, "Made In Gipuzkoa" published to help anyone across global football who cared to read it, learn from it and apply the concepts.

One of its key phrases, again sounding from another age, is: "The essence of this model is the person, not just the footballer."

The training manual continued: "That boy or girl whose future we don't yet know -- footballer, engineer, doctor, mechanic, lawyer -- is the centre of everything. In this model, each person is a project in themselves, and everything else revolves around them.

"Coaches at Real Sociedad accompany, nurture, and train the boys and girls throughout their entire journey, with stability as the foundation of a model based on trust and patience. In short, to nurture, to train, to guide, to educate. That is the mandate we receive from the community we want to represent, from the families of Gipuzkoa, from Gipuzkoa society in general."

From that old-fashioned, humanistic, community-based football philosophy to the cutthroat, high-tech winner-takes-all ebb and thrust at the top of England's Premier League.

Whatever divides Alonso, Emery, Arteta and Iraola this season, they are all unified by background, beliefs and some values that all of European football could learn from.

stories.headline: 'They smoke us': Why a moon astronaut thinks F1 is ahead of NASA
stories.summary:
150-char blurb
Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman explains why F1's engineering is ahead of NASA's, his admiration for Mercedes and what he learned on the moon.
stories.body:
Somewhere between Earth and the moon, Reid Wiseman encountered a problem. The windows of his Artemis II spacecraft were filthy.

It wasn't a mechanical failure, the haunting bleep of a master alarm or some other unforeseen consequence borne out of attempting to travel further than any human beings in history. Instead, the four astronauts aboard NASA's Artemis II mission had spent so much time with their faces pressed against the glass, gazing in awe at both the diminishing Earth in one direction and the extraordinary lunar landscape growing bigger in the other, that the windows were covered in smudges.

"We were looking out at Earth and we were looking out at the moon all the time," Wiseman told ESPN. "Victor [Glover], my pilot, made a comment when we got into our first orbit of Earth, he's like, 'that's the last time Reid ever looked inside [the spacecraft].'

- Nate Saunders on the contradictions of Austin's COTA

- How Kimi Antonelli can win the title in Mexico City

- Fernando Alonso slams 'low quality bottom third of the grid'

"We had to do a photo analysis of the windows so that the geology team could make sure there was no damage, or if they were seeing blemishes on lunar photography, they could relay it back. And I was looking at the windows before I got the camera out to do the survey, and I called down to Mission Control and said, 'hey, first, I need to clean them, because the amount of grease marks from our noses and foreheads on the windows, it was just completely covered.'"

For the commander of the first crewed mission to the moon in more than half a century, it was an understandable distraction. The view was unlike anything he had experienced before, even during his previous six-month stint aboard the International Space Station.

"We're human. Making sure the spacecraft is operating is of the prime of importance. But right underneath that is absorbing the experience. The thing that struck me most looking at the Earth is it got very small, and then it got, like, that big," Wiseman said, pushing his thumb and index finger almost completely together.

"But really looking at the moon was the three-dimensionality of everything. You're not looking through an atmosphere. Everything is crystal clear, everything. The blacks, the craters, the bumps, the sun hitting the crater rim, it was profoundly crystal clear, and all four of us felt that exact same thing. Your brain was having trouble processing the clarity with which we were seeing this three-dimensional moon right there out of the window."

Spine-tingling stuff, even if here it was slightly off-topic, at least in an official capacity.

The premise of Wiseman's interview time with ESPN was not primarily about space. Although when you're talking to someone who has travelled a quarter of a million miles from Earth, how could it be about anything else?

Sitting at Austin's Circuit of the Americas, Wiseman was not wearing the orange spacesuit of Artemis II, nor the familiar dark blue of NASA, but the white of Mercedes' Formula 1 team's team kit. Six months after returning from his historic journey around the moon, Wiseman became an ambassador for the German manufacturer. Last year, he and his daughter had attended the United States Grand Prix on general admission tickets. Then, for all intents and purposes, Wiseman was just another person baking in the Texas sun with thousands of other people. Returning a year later he can boast that he's one of just nine living humans to have seen the far side of the moon with their own eyes.

The setting of the interview prompted an obvious question.

How does NASA compare to Formula 1? The answer was surprising.

"Oh, they crush us," he replied. "I mean, the level of engineering here, they smoke us."

Wiseman's view is rooted in the priorities of the two disciplines. NASA places a premium on proven technology and backup systems, even if that means carrying additional weight into space to ensure the mission objectives are met. Formula 1, meanwhile, is about the relentless pursuit of performance and pushing the boundaries of engineering in search of even the smallest advantage. As we spoke, we were surrounded by Mercedes' race operation -- engineers, mechanics, media team, performance coaches, who have impressed him as much as the technology.

"In spaceflight, what we really need is tried and true, redundancy, and we can accept a little bit of a mass penalty," he said. "Here, they're just pushing everything to the next level, and just every single thing is ... it's not just the cars, it's the humans. You know, everybody's walking around with WHOOP straps, and monitoring everything about themselves. They're all basically athletes. They're all going all in at all times. I love the way they deal with human performance and mechanical performance."

The competition aspect of Formula 1 -- which pits Mercedes against 10 other teams every race -- is always going to skew a comparison between Antonelli's world and Wiseman's world. For the Artemis II commander, it's the hunger to win that sets Formula 1 apart.

"At the end of the day in our work, there's a really large team of experts that sit just under the fanfare, but are the ones that are the true heroes that have the real courage. And then on top are these people who are willing to push the envelope a little bit and go.

"What is a little different for us is I have a crew of four people that are together in the spacecraft and working to try to make this mission the best it can be. In these cars, it is George [Russell] going all in, killer instinct ... Kimi [Antonelli] going all in, killer instinct. Occasionally they might meet in a corner and then I'm like, 'oh dear god, let's get through the corner.'"

For Mercedes, that focus on performance has seen the German team climb back to the pinnacle of the sport this year. Wiseman was speaking ahead of a U.S. Grand Prix which saw Kimi Antonelli move to the verge of becoming the sport's youngest-ever world champion at 20 years old.

This weekend, he will almost certainly wrap it up in Mexico City.

Wiseman can remember his interaction with Antonelli in 2024, before he had even started racing in Formula 1. Even then, Wiseman could see traits that have helped propel Antonelli to the brink of history.

"I met Kimi briefly when he was touring the Johnson Space Centre, and he invited me to a race when he was there," Wiseman said.

"[He was] 17. When I met him, the first thing I thought was how astonishingly humble and down to earth he was. But at the same time, he's a little goofy, which I love, but he's just curious about everything. We were touring with a few other drivers, but Kimi was asking every question about every single thing, whether he needed the information or not. Those are the people I try to latch on to because that curiosity is so powerful.

"You walk around, why is that cloud there? Why is that bird flying? How is it doing that? Why are these tyres better than these tyres?"

Antonelli's rise came after a rollercoaster rookie season in 2025. The young Italian has this year made a lot of the support network Mercedes put around him - team boss Toto Wolff's arm-over-the-shoulder approach to some of Antonelli's early mistakes were key. So has been the oversight of his race engineer, Peter Bonnington, who brought with him the experience of working in the same role with Lewis Hamilton.

Even here, Wiseman cannot help but point to where the two worlds overlap in some way.

"I chuckle at the way Bono and Kimi talk [on the radio]. It feels exactly like us in space, where we'll say something to the engineering team, and then when we unkey the mic, the engineering team will be like, 'they don't know what they're talking about', and then they'll come up with an answer for us, and they'll send it back. I love hearing that.

"I love it when the engineers and the drivers joke around on the radio, and you can just tell. It's just a great relationship."

Wiseman's link-up with Mercedes is a unique thing, but he feels right at home. He admits he was never one of those "crazy space kids" who could name every Apollo astronaut or had Neil Armstrong as a boyhood hero. But there was an interest in racing from a young age. He grew up going to NASCAR races with his father in Delaware, although they never did fulfill their dream of watching an Indy 500 together. His first chance to see Formula 1 in person was in 2023, invited by McLaren and Mercedes.

Wiseman admits he initially wondered what to expect from the "terrifying Toto Wolff," but has since come to admire the culture the Mercedes boss has established.

"What really struck me was, he's actually not scary, he's hilarious in his own humour. What I noticed as we were here, if you look around this place, there's no flash, it's just professionalism. 'We were going to go get the job done, and not just on the track.' It's the way they take care of the fans, the way they take care of the sponsors, the way they take care of the engineering team."

As he continued, Wiseman gestured over to Mercedes reserve driver Fred Vesti for another anecdote. "I went out for a run this morning with the engineers and did a swim down in Austin with them, and then I couldn't keep up on the way home, so I ran with Fred Vesti. He hung back and ran with me. The culture here always comes from the top. You can just tell Toto has one hell of a racing team that also knows how to take care of people."

Here is where he thinks NASA can learn a great deal from Formula 1's super-active team members. "Astronauts have to put a pretty good premium on our own health and physical conditioning, because we're going to be weightless, and our bones and our muscles are going to waste during the mission.

"So we put a big premium on that. We don't put as big of a premium on our support team and making sure they are at their highest level, and I think we can raise their level of expertise. They spend a lot of their days sitting in chairs, analysing data, and most of them would probably be upset if I said, let's go run three miles, but I think we can elevate the human performance, and we should really look at that. Because you look around in this team, everybody is fit, they're hungry, they're getting after it, and I think we can elevate the team [at NASA]."

Wiseman was brought to Mercedes to tell these kinds of stories. His role is to work with team partners, sponsors and guests to explain the overlap between the two worlds and, of course, to tell captivating stories about his own experiences. It's easy to see what he brings to the table. Had our interview not already overrun its 15-minute slot, it would have been easy to have kept going and going. "Toto likes the way I communicate," he said. "I think [guests] also like hearing stories of four humans that have gone further from Earth than anyone else. And I think there's just a lot of good storytelling and a sense of adventure that comes from that."

Inevitably, of course, our conversation drifted back to space.

Wiseman's anecdotes do not end with the stories he can tell verbally. At one point, he reached for his phone to show a picture with legendary Apollo-era flight director Gene Kranz, now 91, and Apollo 13 astronaut Fred Haise, taken earlier that week. Scattered through his camera roll were photographs he had taken himself of the moon from inside the spacecraft, through those smudged windows. Not a bad collection of snaps to have at your fingertips.

The Artemis II mission captivated a worldwide audience. In one of its most poignant moments, Wiseman's crewmates surprised him by naming a lunar crater in honour of his late wife, Carroll. But while millions of people followed their every move from Earth, the four astronauts were experiencing something rather different.

It is only since returning home that Wiseman has begun to appreciate just how much the mission meant to those watching.

"One thing that has been so rewarding is fame is not really that fun. I don't know how Kimi and George deal with that," he said. "But I was at an airport over in Europe the other day, and a dad came over to me and said, 'Hey, my daughter thinks you're Reid Wiseman. Are you?' And I said, yes, I am.

"And he turns to her, and this 10-year-old girl from the Philippines comes running over and just gave me the biggest hug. She knew everything about Christina, everything about Victor, everything about Jeremy.

"And I took this little medallion off my backpack and gave it to her, and she was so emotional. That stuff just is, it's all we could have ever wished for."

It was one of countless stories Wiseman and his crewmates have been hearing since they returned, providing a new perspective on a journey they are still coming to terms with themselves.

"We were all together three weeks ago. And we hadn't been together in a few weeks, and we were like, how's everything going? What are you feeling right now?

"And we all have this common feeling of we're starting to understand that we experienced this mission, but Earth experienced it. And now we're loving hearing the stories.

"Now that we've kind of processed the mission, we're listening to the stories from our friends at launch, when Carroll Crater was named, the amount of emotion that was involved in that. People were waking up and turning on the YouTube channel to see where are they today, what's going on.

"And we realised we went on a mission, but actually Earth kind of did too."
